title: After the incident: close the route, then test it
body_md:
## Find the pipe, not only the puddle

You changed the password the same hour, and the puddle is gone. That tells you nothing about the pipe behind the wall, which may still be dripping: a forwarding rule, a spare recovery address, an app you never approved. Once the emergency is over, turn the timeline of the incident into a repair list, and put first whatever let the attacker in.

Don’t rotate every password just because one account sent a phishing message. Pick out the credentials that were shared, reused, stored on a device someone else controlled, or reachable through the compromised mailbox, and change those from known-good devices on the provider’s official pages. A password manager can generate a unique replacement for each. If its own account or device was exposed, though, secure that first.

### Accounts and recovery paths

Review active sessions and sign them out where the provider allows it. Check the recovery email and phone, backup codes, mail forwarding, filters, connected apps and app-specific passwords. Deleting one visible forwarding rule is not enough if another authorized app or a recovery address still gives access. Choose the strongest sign-in the service practically offers. Passkeys and security keys built on WebAuthn/FIDO2 resist phishing better than codes typed by hand, though what is available, and how recovery works, differs from service to service. If SMS is the only method on offer, use it rather than going without a second factor, and secure your carrier account. Keep a backup way in, so that losing one device does not lock you out.

### Devices and money

Install supported security updates on every device used in the incident. Once you have documented what happened, remove remote-support software you don’t recognize, along with unfamiliar browser extensions. For suspected malware, use reputable security tools or ask the manufacturer or your employer for help. A clean scan is reassuring, not proof, and a managed work device follows the employer’s procedure. If a card number was exposed, follow the issuer’s instructions on replacement and monitoring; a problem with transfers out of an account may call for different controls. Keep reading statements and alerts as the weeks go by. A US credit freeze or a Russian loan self-ban covers only the new credit it was built for.

### A short follow-up checklist

- Confirm affected passwords are unique and recovery contacts are yours.
- Review sessions, forwarding and connected apps again after several days.
- If your phone number was involved, ask your carrier about number-transfer protection.
- Turn on bank transaction alerts, and track the open dispute or replacement card.
- Where it fits, set a later date to go over the incident record with someone you trust or your workplace team.

### What “done” looks like

Keep a short ledger with one line per exposure: what was exposed, the control you changed, how you confirmed it, who owns it, and the date to check again. A few days later, recheck that recovery contacts and forwarding are still as you left them, and follow any bank or provider case until it has an outcome. Closing is a decision based on the risks you know about, not a certainty that every unseen action was found. Keep a way to reopen the case if a late alert or a fraudulent account turns up.

widget_config.goal: Turn the way the attacker got in into a repair and follow-up checklist you can verify, knowing the limits of each control.
widget_config.today_action: Open the official settings of one important account and check its recovery email, recovery phone and active sessions. Write down any change in a private checklist.
widget_config.scope: General hardening for individuals. Authenticator options, device support, banking controls and credit measures differ by provider and country. The people in the examples are invented.

blocks.title: New password, same leak
blocks.situation: After an email takeover, Nika changes her password. A week later, a hidden forwarding rule is still sending copies of her mail to an address outside her mailbox.
blocks.analysis: The new password closed one path and left what the attacker had planted. Nika deletes the rule, goes through connected apps, recovery contacts and sessions, and looks at all of it again a few days later to be sure it held.

blocks.title: An app on the list that you did install
blocks.situation: A calendar app shows up in Luis’s account permissions. He installed it himself, and he checks its exact permissions in the provider’s settings.
blocks.analysis: An app on the list is not automatically the attacker’s. Luis can keep an app he needs and understands, and remove stale grants. Revoking everything indiscriminately could break his work.

blocks.title: The route that is still open
blocks.setup: An invented case: a mailbox was used to send fake invoices. The password has been changed, but the incident review isn’t finished.

steps.prompt: The password is new. Which settings do you open next?

choices.text: The profile page, to make sure the name and photo still look right.
choices.consequence: It says nothing about how access persists.
choices.explanation: Look first at the controls that grant access.

choices.text: Forwarding rules, recovery contacts, sessions and connected apps.
choices.consequence: You are hunting for the access paths that remain.
choices.explanation: A password change alone can leave delegated access in place.

steps.prompt: A calendar app you know appears in the list. What do you do?

choices.text: Verify the owner and permissions, then keep or revoke it depending on whether you really need it.
choices.consequence: Legitimate access keeps working and excess access shrinks.
choices.explanation: Don’t call a connected app malicious on its name alone.

choices.text: Report the app as the attacker’s handiwork.
choices.consequence: You may brand an ordinary tool as the culprit.

steps.prompt: You suspect the laptop had remote-support software on it. How do you change your credentials?

choices.text: On that same laptop, which someone may still control.
choices.consequence: The new secrets could be captured as you type them.
choices.explanation: A new password typed on a watched machine may not stay secret.

choices.text: From a trusted device: remove the software with reputable help, then review the affected credentials.
choices.consequence: The new passwords are less likely to be seen.
choices.explanation: Trust in the device matters when you rotate credentials.

steps.prompt: What makes the review complete enough to close?

choices.text: Documented controls, confirmations and follow-up dates, and a plan to reopen the case if new evidence appears.
choices.consequence: The decision can be traced and revised.
choices.explanation: No checklist can prove an attacker did nothing unseen.

choices.text: Declaring permanent safety because one scan came back clean.
choices.consequence: Unknown paths or delayed fraud may still be there.
choices.explanation: A scan is not a guarantee.

blocks.debrief: Repair the specific route, look at the neighboring recovery paths, and confirm the result later. Go back and take the other choices; a finished checklist is a reasoned snapshot, not a promise.

questions.prompt: A password is changed, but a stranger’s recovery email remains. Is the account secured?

choices.text: Yes. A password change removes all other access.
choices.explanation: The recovery address can win control back.

choices.text: No. Remove the unauthorized recovery path and review sessions.
choices.explanation: Both the credential and the recovery route matter.

questions.prompt: A service offers SMS as its only second factor. What is the practical choice?

choices.text: Use SMS as offered, protect your carrier account, and watch for stronger options.
choices.explanation: A second factor still helps, even though SMS carries SIM-swap risk.

choices.text: Turn off multi-factor sign-in (MFA) until a security key is supported.
choices.explanation: That throws away protection you can have today.

questions.prompt: A clean malware scan proves the device was never controlled. True or false?

choices.explanation: Scans have limits and can’t establish a device’s whole history.

choices.text: False. Treat the scan as one signal and get trusted help when needed.
choices.explanation: A scan finds only what it knows how to look for. What you do next depends on what was exposed and who owns the device.
